  public inspection at the time the records are distributed to all, or a majority of all, members of the City Council,

Due to health recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of California
Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA), and the declared state of emergency
wherein social distancing measures have been imposed or recommended, the CITY OF
AVALON’S CITY COUNCIL and PLANNING COMMISSION MEETINGS SHALL GENERALLY
BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The general public may attend the meeting in
the Council Chambers however must adhere to social distancing requirements. The public is
encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes while practicing social
distancing.

Council Chambers are open to a maximum 30 members of the general public. Once the Council
Chambers reach maximum occupancy, the general public may participate in Oral
Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by waiting in the City
Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the appropriate time. No one will be
admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-1 9. Additionally,
the general public may participate in Oral Communication and address the City Council on an
agenda items by providing comments via Zoom or by sending comments to

2.  Warrants

  o Warrants in the amount of $667,366.73.
  o One payroll in the amount of $207,396.72.
  o Three electronic fund transfers totaling $139,919.21.
  Recommended Action
  Approve total expenditures for May 30, 2022 through June 10, 2022 totaling
  $1,014,682.66.

3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City Council Meetings
  Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  At the November 16, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council made findings pursuant
  to Assembly Bill 361 to continue to meet remotely. To continue this practice, it is required,
  that the City Council determine that the COVID-1 9 state of emergency proclaimed by the
  Governor still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue
  to have teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or
  recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and
  that as a result of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent
  risks to the health or safety of attendees. Because these findings must be made every
  thirty (30) days, the City Council will have to make these findings at its upcoming July 19,
  2022 meeting and thirty (30) days thereafter.
  Recommended Action
  Determine that the COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by the Governor still exists
  and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue to have
  teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
  measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and that as a result
  of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the
  health or safety of attendees.

4.  Law Enforcement Services Agreement with Los Angeles County
  Annually, the City Council submits an authorization form establishing the annual fee for
  Los Angeles County to provide law enforcement services to the City. The estimated cost
  of services in FY 22-23 totals $1,659,588.78.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution notifying the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors of the City’s
  desire to receive specified law enforcement services from the Los Angeles County
  Sheriff’s (LASD) office, authorizing the expenditure of COPS Grant Funds and authorize
  the City Manager to execute the Service Level Authorization Form (SH-AD 575) for FY
  22-23.

5.  Resolution Adopting List of Proiects for Annual SB1 Allocation
  In 2017, Senate Bill 1 (SB1) was enacted to provide new funding to address basic
  maintenance, rehabilitation and critical safety needs of local streets and roads in addition
  for other transportation needs statewide. Staff identified the City of Avalon Five Corner
  Comprehensive Pedestrian Project as the project that would provide the greatest benefit
  for the community with the upcoming fiscal year allocation.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 21, 2022
PAGE 4

  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution establishing a project list for Fiscal Year 2022-23 to be funded by SB1
  —The Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017.

6.  2022 Conflict of Interest Code-Biennial Notice
  The Political Reform Act requires the City to notify all departments and advisory bodies,
  commissions, and committees that have previously adopted conflict of interest codes that
  a review must be conducted every other year.
  Recommended Action
  Direct the City Clerk to notify all City Departments and advisory bodies that have
  previously adopted conflict of interest codes, of the biennial review requirements for such
  conflict of interest codes. Require all departments and advisory bodies that have
  previously adopted conflict of interest codes to review such conflict of interest codes and
  report to the City Council any amendments, or report that no amendments are necessary,
  no later than October 3, 2022.

PUBLIC HEARING

7.  Public Hearing and Submittal of Property Related Fees to Los Angeles County for FY22-
  23 Property Tax Roll Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Fees
  —

  For the County to collect the fees for the City, the City Council is required to hold a noticed
  public hearing, where customers subject to the fees are afforded an opportunity to make
  objections or protests to collecting the fees on the property tax roll.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open a public hearing on whether to collect the annual trash collection service fees,
  grease collection service fees, sewer user fees, and saltwater charges, on the property
  tax roll by the County of Los Angeles. 2. If no majority protest is filed, close the public
  hearing and adopt four resolution adopting reports of the annual trash collection services
  fees, grease collection service fees, sewer user fees, and saltwater charges. 3. Direct the
  City Clerk to request Los Angeles County to place the fees on the FY 2022/23 Property
  Tax Roll.

8.  Public Hearing for Approval of Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Community Development Block
  Grant (CDBG) Funds, and Re-Allocation of the balance of Fiscal Year 2021-22 Funds
  A Public Hearing is required to receive comments on the proposed use of the FY 2022-
  2023 CDBG Funds. The City proposes to use reserve CDBG funds for the amount of
  $40,000 and re-allocate FY 2021-2022 funds in the amount of $71,000 for a total project
  cost of $111,000 for the ADA Curb and Ramp Project.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open the Public Hearing, accept comments. 2. Close the Public Hearing. 3. Authorize
  the City Manager to approve the allocation of Fiscal Year 2022-2023 CDBG Funds and
  re-allocation the balance of Fiscal Year 2021-2022 CDBG Funds.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 21, 2022
PAGE 5

9.  Appeal Planning Commission Action 22-01 of PC #2783 Approving a Setback Variance
  at 261 E. Whittley
  On April 20, 2022, the Planning Commission of the City of Avalon took action on a request
  for approval of a Site Plan and a Setback Variance at 261 E. Whittley for the ongoing
  remodel of a duplex in the Medium Density Residential zone. On May 3, 2022 Charles
  Canby, and other surrounding property owners, filed a timely appeal of the Planning
  Commission’s decision, requesting that the City Council hear the Project at a public
  hearing. A public hearing was opened on June 8, 2022, the meeting was continued to
  June 21, 2022.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open the Public Hearing to hear public comment. 2. Close the Public Hearing. 3.
  Continue the matter for hearing on another date before itself.

GENERAL BUSINESS

10.  Fiscal Year 2022 Proposed Budget Amendments
  The proposed budget amendments either relate to required pass-through expenditures,
  with the increased expenditures offset by increased revenues, or relate to planned
  contributions to the City’s landfill trust account included as part of the rate study.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution authorizing the proposed budget amendments as outlined in this
  report.

11.  Proposed Fiscal Year 2022-23 Budget
  Based on the input received during budget study sessions, Staff is presenting the
  proposed Fiscal Year 2022-23 Operating and Capital Budget for City Council to review
  and consider for adoption. The proposed budget also includes updates to the City’s
  Budget and Fiscal Policies, which includes the Statement of Investment Policy, for review
  and adoption.
  Recommended Action
  Continue discussing the proposed Fiscal Year 2022-23 Budget. If consensus, adopt the
  resolution establishing the City budget for Fiscal Year 2022-23.

12.  Approval of Encroachment Permit for a retaining wall at the Zane Grey Hotel
  The Chimes Tower Investment Inc., dba the Zane Grey Hotel, is requesting approval of
  an encroachment permit for in kind replacement of existing retaining walls/landscaping
  features within a portion of the public right of way at 199 Chimes Tower Road.
  Recommended Action
  Approve encroachment permit for a retaining wall at 199 Chimes Tower Road, the Zane
  Grey Hotel, and authorize City Staff to negotiate with the property owners to determine
  the amounts of the required bond and liability insurance.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 21, 2022
PAGE 6

13.  Transportation Permit Operation Plan Leyva’s Electric Bike Rental
  .—

  On May 3, 2022, the City Council approved a transfer of a Transportation Permit for 30
  electric bicycles to Martin Leyva. Though the permit transfer was approved, Leyva was
  required to return to City Council once he had identified a brick-and-mortar location for
  his operations.
  Recommended Action
  1. Consider the operations plan for Leyva’s Electric Bike Rentals to operate up to 30
  electric bicycles for rental and guided tours at 233 Sumner Avenue. 2. If consensus for
  approval, require Leyva to adhere to all conditions set forth in the Avalon Municipal Code
  and Resolution 21-07.

CLOSED SESSION

  —

  Case Number: 2OLBCVOO291

SUBJECT:  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City
  Council Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Determine that the COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed
by the Governor still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue
to have teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and that as a result of the
COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health or safety
of attendees.

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionally, the Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings,
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body’s members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda. that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. Newly enacted AB 361 provides an exception to these
procedures in order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including
the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsom’s Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021, Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EO N-29-20 would sunset on September 30, 2021.

On September 10, 2021, the Legislature adopted AS 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16, 2021. Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required under AR 361

Under AS 361, the City Council can hold virtual meetings without providing notice of the City
Council’s teleconference location if the City Council makes the determination that there is a
Governor-proclaimed state of emergency, which the City Council will consider in their
determination, and one of two secondary criteria listed below exists:

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; or

65059.00000\3452048 1.1
   2. The City Council determines that requiring a meeting in person would present an
  imminent risk to the health or safety of attendees.

COVID-19 continues to present an imminent threat to the health or safety of members of the
public, and the Governor’s declaration of a COVID-19 emergency still exists. Although vaccines
are now widely available, many people in the State and County are still not fully vaccinated and
remain susceptible to infection. The disease can still spread rapidly through person-to-person
contact and those in close proximity. Further, more contagious variants of the disease are now
present in the State and County, the most predominant of which is a new variant of the Omnicron
variant. The County of Los Angeles recently re-instituted some mandates given the rise in cases
and deaths nationally. The City’s economy is dependent upon visitors to the island, the presence
of which, increases the likelihood of transmission of the disease. Also, having members of the
public attend council meetings at locations where council members are in attendance due to their
desire to avoid exposure to COVID-1 9 poses an imminent risk to the health or safety of attendees.

Re-Authorization is Required Within 30 Days

The City Council made the findings listed above at its June 8, 2022 City Council meeting.
Consistent with the provisions of Government Code Section 54953(e), the findings must be made
every 30 days “after teleconferencing for the first time” under AB 361. Thus, if the City Council
desires to continue to meet remotely without having to post the location of each teleconference
location, the City Council must again find that the COVID-19 emergency still exists and that one
of the two following findings can be made: that state or local officials have imposed or
recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, or, that a
result of the COVID-1 9 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health
or safety of attendees. Because these findings must be made every thirty (30) days, the City
Council will have to make these findings at its upcoming July 19, 2022 meeting and thirty (30)
days thereafter.

It is recommended that the City Council make these findings.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City Council will
have to follow the Brown Act provisions that existed prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council make the findings under AB 361 at its July 5, 2022
City Council meeting.

SUBJECT:  Law Enforcement Services Agreement with Los Angeles County

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a resolution notifying the Los Angeles County Board of
Supervisors of the City’s desire to receive specified law enforcement services from the Los
Angeles County Sheriff’s (LASD) office, authorizing the expenditure of COPS Grant Funds and
authorize the City Manager to execute the Service Level Authorization Form (SH-AD 575) for
FY 22-23.

REPORT SUMMARY: The attached authorization form establishes the annual fee for Los
Angeles County to provide law enforcement services to the City for FY 22-23. The estimated
cost of services in FY 22-23 totals $1,659,588.78.

During the June 1, 2021 meeting of the City Council, the City Council authorized the City
Manager to execute the authorization form for FY 21-22 totaling $1,481,628.00.

LASD works with 46 contract cities. Unlike other cites, the City of Avalon receives a special
“Catalina Deputy” rate for services. From FY 21-22 to FY 22-23 the “Catalina Deputy” rate
increased from $266,960 to $271,836. The “Catalina Deputy” rate is an approximate $29,449
savings per deputy over other cities.

Additionally, LASD does not charge the City a salary for its Station Commander, six additional
deputies, tour 911 emergency dispatchers, a portion of a jailer salary, use of various public
safety equipment including all department vehicles and boats or any other supplemental
  —
  —

services.

For FY 22-23, LASD proposed increasing the number of paid deputies from 5 to 5.5. This
change accounts for approximately $135,918 of the overall increase to the contract. With this
proposed amendment, the Station Commander will have greater flexibility with schedule and
more manpower to support the City’s needs.

Per the terms of the contract, the City of Avalon has the option to request additional reserve
deputies to provide public safety services on an as needed basis. The City does not pay these
reserve deputies a salary, but the City does cover their travel, hotel accommodations and
reimbursements for meals. Historically, the City has hired reserve deputies on popular
weekends throughout the year as well as during cruise ship days. The fees for these reserve
deputies are not included in the regular contract. Since the beginning of the COVID-19
situation, the City has not utilized reserve deputies as much as in previous years.
 From FY 2122 to FY 22-23 the total contract cost is projected to increase by approximately
$177,930.78. There are two elements of the contract: cost of services and the hability trust
fund allocation. The cost of services increased most significantly due to the addition of 0.5
deputies. The liability trust fund is the Contract Cities self-insurance and is allocated to
members by multiplying the services provided by an approved percentage. The liability trust
fund cost allocation percentage is 11% of the service cost and will slightly increase due to the
additional deputy.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Contract amount of $1659558.78 is budgeted in the FY 22-23 Budget, in
the General Fund account 10240-5110.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will not have
an executed contract with the Los Angeles Sheriff’s Department.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Execute authorization form and send to Contract City Law
Enforcement Services.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: Pursuant to the Brown Act.

SUBJECT:  Resolution Adopting List of Projects for Annual SB1 Allocation

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a resolution establishing a project list for Fiscal Year
2022-23 to be funded by SB1 The Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017.
  —

REPORT SUMMARY: In 2017, Senate Bill 1 (SB1) was enacted to provide new funding to
address basic maintenance, rehabilitation and critical safety needs of local streets and roads in
addition for other transportation needs statewide.

One of the requirements of the program is that each agency must adopt a list of projects for
their annual formula allocation that is submitted to the California Transportation Commission.

The City’s estimated allocation for Fiscal Year 2022-23 is $87,949. Staff identified the Five
Corners Complete Street Project, known as the City of Avalon Five Corner Comprehensive
Pedestrian Project as the project that would provide the greatest benefit for the community with
the upcoming fiscal year allocation. This determination was based on the City’s need to
provide matching funds to the existing grant funds.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: N/A

FISCAL IMPACTS: The addition of $87,949 to Account No.10575-6547 for the current fiscal
year.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION:  The City would not
receive allocations of SB1 funds.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Submit the approved project list and resolution to the California
Transportation Commission through the CaISMART system by July 1, 2022.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT:  This item was properly listed on the
posted agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

SUBJECT:  2022 Conflict of Interest Code-Biennial Notice

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Direct the City Clerk to notify all City Departments and
advisory bodies that have previously adopted conflict of interest codes, of the biennial
review requirements for such conflict of interest codes. Require all departments and
advisory bodies that have previously adopted conflict of interest codes to review such
conflict of interest codes and report to the City Council any amendments, or report that
no amendments are necessary, no later than October 3, 2022.

REPORT SUMMARY: The Political Reform Act requires the City to notify all
departments and advisory bodies, commissions, and committees that have previously
adopted conflict of interest codes. Government Code Section 87306.5, effective 1990,
requires that each local government agency conduct a review of its conflict of interest
codes every other year. If any amendments are necessary, the proposed amendment(s)
should be submitted to the City Council no later than October 3, 2022.

FISCAL IMPACTS: None.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Not Aligned.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: To ensure
conflict of interest codes remain current and accurate, each local agency is required to
review its code at least every even-numbered year. If the City does not, it will not be in
compliance.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Proceed with City Council’s direction.

the posted agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

SUBJECT:  Public Hearing and Submittal of Property Related Fees to Los Angeles
  County for FY22-23 Property Tax Roll Sewer. Saltwater, and Solid
  —

  Waste Fees

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Open a public hearing on whether to collect the annual
trash collection service fees, grease collection service fees, sewer user fees, and saltwater
charges, on the property tax roll by the County of Los Angeles. 2. If no majority protest is filed,
close the public hearing and adopt four resolution adopting reports of the annual trash
collection services fees, grease collection service fees, sewer user fees, and saltwater
charges. 3. Direct the City Clerk to request Los Angeles County to place the fees on the FY
2022/23 Property Tax Roll.

REPORT SUMMARY: At the June 1, 2021 City Council Meeting, City Council adopted the
findings of a cost of service and rates study for sewer, saltwater, and solid waste services,
which assessed the adequacy of the revenues to maintain the physical integrity of the systems
to comply with all Federal and State regulations pursuant to Proposition 218. The proposed
rates were designed to produce the minimum revenue needed to cover projected operating
costs, including direct operating expenses, administrative costs, and ongoing capital
improvement repairs, replacements and upgrades. A copy of the Comprehensive Sewer,
Saltwater, and Solid Waste Rate Study has been included as an attachment to this report.

For the County to collect the fees for the City, the City Council is required to hold a noticed
public hearing, where customers subject to the fees are afforded an opportunity to make
objections or protests to collecting the fees on the property tax roll. If objections or protests
are not made by the owners of a majority of the separate parcels subject to the fees, the City
Council may adopt the reports of the annual fees and direct the City Clerk to file the reports
with the Los Angeles County Auditor and request the fees be placed on the County property
tax roll. Collecting the fees on the property tax rolls saves the City the costs of billing the fees
itself. The County charges $0.25 per fee per parcel.

City Staff is proposing the following rate increases for the Fiscal Year 2022-2023:

  •  Sewer +7.0%
  •  Saltwater +2.5%
  •  Solid Waste +11.5%
  •  Grease Collection +11.5%
 The proposed increases to rates are necessary to adequately fund capital improvements to
existing infrastructure and to develop and maintain adequate reserve levels. In particular, the
Solid Waste fund proposed rate increases reflect additional revenues required to fund new
state recycling mandates, permitting for potential landfill expansion, and contributions to landfill
trust fund for future closure and post-closure costs. The rate increase for Sewer and Saltwater
services are aligned with the rates included in the adopted study. The adopted study had
included a 195% increase for Solid Waste and Grease Collection rates for the upcoming fiscal
year; however, the proposed Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Budget includes a $200,000 subsidy from
the General Fund reserves to lower the required increase to 11.5%. A copy of the current and
proposed fees based on customer classification has been included as an attachment to this
report.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Achieve a structurally balanced budget.

FiSCAL IMPACTS: The rates published in the proposed rate schedule attached will increase
the total Sewer revenue by approximately $190 thousand next year; increase the total
Saltwater revenue by approximately $20 thousand next year, and increase the Solid Waste
revenue by S250 thousand next year.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The Sewer and
Saltwater enterprise funds would have insufficient funds to complete essential capital
improvements to ensure the reliability of the systems. The Solid Waste enterprise fund would
not have sufficient funds to pay for state recycling mandates or landfill closure and post-
closure costs.

FOLLOW UP ACTION:
  • By July 31, 2022 Submit FY22-23 fees to Los Angeles County for collection:
  —

  • Annually review adopted Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid waste rates and cost of service.

posted agenda pursuant to the Brown Act. The notice of Public Hearing was advertised
June 10, 2022 and July 17, 2022.

Subject: City of Avalon Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Rate Study Final Report

Dear Mr. Baker:

HDR Engineering, Inc. (HDR) is pleased to present the final report for the sewer, saltwater,
and solid waste rate study update conducted for the City of Avalon (City). The primary
objective in conducting a rate study for each utility is to establish cost-based and proportional
utility rates, for a five-year period, which is intended to provide adequate and sustainable
funding for each utility’s operational and capital needs. This report outlines the approach,
methodology, findings, and conclusions of the rate study process undertaken for each utility.

This report was developed utilizing the City’s accounting, operating, and historical customer
billing records. HDR has relied upon this information to develop our analyses which formed our
findings, conclusions, and recommendations. At the same time, this study was developed utilizing
generally accepted rate setting principles. The conclusions and recommendations contained
within this report are intended to provide the City with cost-based and equitable utility rates for
its customers.

We appreciate the assistance provided by the City staff, management, and the City Council in the
development of this study.

Introduction
HDR Engineering, Inc. (HDR) was retained by the City of Avalon (City) to perform a comprehensive
sewer, saltwater, and solid waste rate study. The development of this study examines the
adequacy of the existing revenues (rates) for each utility and provides the basis for any

operating and capital (Q&M) needs of each utility. This report describes the overall methodology
used to analyze the City’s rates, for each utility, along with the findings, conclusions, and
recommendations.

 Sewer Cost of Service Analysis
The City’s current sewer rate structure was reviewed to determine the cost-basis and the
proportionality of the sewer rates in the prior study which was completed in 2017 (2017 Study).
It is also important to note that the City does not receive metered water use data, which is
typically used to estimate the wastewater flow in a sewer cost of service analysis for establishing
rates. Therefore, the first step was to define one (1) equivalent dwelling unit (EDU), as the base
for estimated sewer flow. The EDU reflects the estimated flow of the typical single-family
residential customer. In other words, each single-family customer is assigned 1 EDU. The
remaining customers (non-residential) are billed based on a variety of different units such as the
number of rooms, showers, seats, etc., with each billing unit being a proportion of 1 EDU based
on industry standard sewer flow estimates.

The City’s cost of service study analyzed the proportions based on assumed wastewater
contributions, Given the results of the review of the flow assumptions, and resulting proportion
of an EOU, the City’s rates for non-residential customers appeared to be equitable and
proportional. As this analysis has been completed recently, this analysis reviewed the prior
approach, and it was maintained. It is also important to note that the customer characteristics
and the industry standard flow assumptions have not changed since the 2017 study. Given this,
proposed sewer rates can be developed to reflect the overall revenue needs and relationships
between the customer types on an EDU basis as is the City’s current approach.

Rate Adoption
Proposition 218 outlines a specific process to legally adopt and implement the proposed sewer,
saltwater, and solid waste rates. The first requirement is that the rates must be cost-based and
proportional, which is the purpose of completing the rate study. Once the proposed sewer,
saltwater, and solid waste rates have been developed, a public process must be undertaken to
adopt the proposed rates. This began with the presentation of the proposed rates to the Avalon
City Council in April 2021. At this meeting, the City Council directed staff to mail the Proposition
218 notices shown in the Proposition 218 Appendix to the City’s customers which outlines the
  —
  -

proposed changes in rates. The notice also contains the time, date, and location of the public
hearing. The City Council then held a public hearing on June 1, 2021 to discuss the publicly noticed
and proposed rates, Absent sufficient written protest by customers, the City Council moved to
adopt the proposed sewer, saltwater, and solid waste rates as outlined in the customer
notification over the next five-year period.

  Introduction and Overview

1.1 Introduction
The City of Avalon (City) retained HDR Engineering, Inc. (HDR) to perform a rate study for its
sewer, saltwater, and solid waste utilities. The rate study is designed to determine the adequacy
of the existing rates and provide the basis for any adjustments to establish cost-based and
proportional rates. This report describes the methodology, findings, and conclusions of the rate
study process.

The study determined whether existing rates are adequate (sufficient) to meet each of the
utility’s operating and capital expenses with revenues received from customers. Rates set too
low may result in insufficient funds to maintain system integrity. The study provides a cost-basis
and rationale for making appropriate rate adjustments, as well as identifying issues of equity for
some of the utility’s current rates.

1.2 Overview of the Rate Study Process
A study consists of three interrelated analyses performed for each utility. Figure 1- 1 provides an
overview of these analyses.

In a rate study, the revenue requirement analysis is concerned with the overall funding sources
and expenses of the utility. From this analysis, a determination can be made as to the overall
level of adjustment to rates. Next, a cost of service analysis is performed to equitably allocate
and proportionally distribute the revenue requirements to the various types of customers served
(e.g., residential, commercial). Finally, once an overall level of rate adjustment is determined and
an proportional distribution of those costs is completed, the last step of the rate study process is
the design of rates to collect the appropriate level of revenues while considering the other rate

 design goals and objectives of the utility (e.g., revenue stability, conservation). For the City’s
current study, all three analyses were conducted. The results from each task of the rate study,
for the sewer, saltwater, and solid waste utilities, were used as the basis for establishing cost-
based and equitable rates for the City’s customers, It is important to note that the cost of service
analysis from 2017 was reviewed and utilized as the basis for this study.

In developing this study, HDR utilized “generally accepted” rate setting techniques and industry
best practices in the development of the City’s utility rate studies. This report discusses the
methodology, findings and conclusions of the rate study analysis conducted for each utility. This
study has focused on the level of rate revenue needed to fully fund each utility on a standalone
basis, and the rates needed to best generate that level of funding, while meeting the City’s goals
and objectives.

2.1 Introduction
Gaining an understanding of the overall rate setting process and methodologies used is important
in order to better understand the approach to the City’s rate study. This section of the report
provides background information about the rate setting process, including descriptions of
generally accepted principles, types of utilities, methods for determining revenue requirements,
and rate design. This should provide the reader with a better understanding of the detailed
analyses presented in following sections of the report and the basis for our conclusions and
reco m me ndatio ns.

2.2 Generally Accepted Rate Setting Principles
As a practical matter, utilities should consider setting their rates around some generally accepted
or global principles and guidelines. Utility rates should be:
•  Cost-based, equitable, and set at a level that meets the utility’s full revenue requirement
•  Easy to understand and administer
•  Designed to conform with generally accepted rate setting techniques
•  Stable in their ability to provide adequate revenues for meeting the utility’s financial,
  operating, and regulatory requirements
•  Established at a level that is stable from year-to-year from a customer’s perspective
•  Established in compliance with State law

2.3 Types of Utilities
Utilities are generally divided into two types:
1. Public utilities are owned by a city, county, or special district, and are operated at zero profit
Public utilities are capitalized or financed by issuing debt and recovering funds from customers
through direct capital contributions or user rates. Public or municipal utilities are typically exempt
from state and federal income taxes. A publicly elected City Council or Board of Directors usually
regulates public utilities.
2. Private utilities are “for profit” enterprises and are owned by a private company and/or
  shareholders. The shareholders are, in essence, the owners of the private utility. Therefore,
  the owners of a private utility may not be customers or local citizens, but rather numerous
  individuals or shareholders spread across the United States. A private utility is capitalized by
  issuing stock to the general public.

Private utilities are taxable entities. Given their for-profit status, their rates and operations are
generally regulated by a state public utility commission or other regulatory body.

As a point of reference, the City’s utilities are public (municipal) utilities and the analyses have
been based on the methodology generally utilized by for public utilities.

2.4 Determining the Revenue Requirement
Because public and private utilities have very different administrative and financial
characteristics, their methods differ for determining revenue requirements and setting rates. A
discussion of these rate setting differences are provided below.

2.4.1  Public Utilities
Most public utilities use the “cash basis”1 approach for establishing their revenue requirement
and setting rates. This approach conforms to most public utility budgetary requirements and the
calculation is easy to understand. A public utility:
•  Totals its cash expenditures for a period of time to determine required revenues
•  Adds operation and maintenance (O&M) expenses to any applicable taxes or transfer
  payments to determine total operating expenses. Operation and maintenance expenses
  include the materials, electricity, labor, supplies, etc. needed to keep the utility functioning.
•  Calculates capital costs by adding debt service payments (principal and interest) to capital
  improvements financed with rate revenues, In lieu of including capital improvements
  financed with rate revenues, a utility sometimes includes depreciation expense to stabilize
  annual revenue requirement.

Under the cash basis approach, the sum of the capital and operating expenses equals the utility’s
revenue requirement during any period of time (see Table 2- 1).

Note that the two portions of the capital expense component (debt service and capital
improvements financed from rates) are necessary under the cash basis approach because utilities
generally cannot finance all their capital facilities with long-term debt. An exception occurs if a
public utility provides service to a wholesale or contract customer. In this situation, a public utility
could use the “utility basis” approach (see below) to earn a fair return on its investment.

recoded when cash is disbursed.

3.2 Determining the Sewer Utility Revenue Requirement
The revenue requirement is the first analytical step in the comprehensive rate study process. This
analysis determines the adequacy of the overall sewer rates, at current rate levels, to recover
sufficient revenues to fund the utility’s projected total annual operations and maintenance
expenses and capital-related costs incurred to meet the various aspects of providing the utility’s
services. From this analysis, a determination can be made as to the overall level of rate
adjustment needed to provide adequate and prudent funding for both operating and capital
needs.

In developing the revenue requirement, it was assumed the sewer utility must financially “stand
on its own” and be properly funded. As a result, the revenue requirement as developed herein
assumes the full and proper funding needed to operate and maintain the system on a financially
sound and prudent basis, This includes maintaining adequate reserve levels, prudently funding
annual repair and replacement needs (rate-funded capital), and meeting other industry standard
financial metrics (e.g., debt service coverage), where applicable. Provided below is a more
detailed discussion of the development of the revenue requirement analysis for the City’s sewer
utility.

3.2.1  Determining the Time Period and Approach
The first step in calculating the revenue requirement for the sewer utility was to establish a test
period, or the time period to review the revenue requirement analysis. For this study, the
revenue requirement was developed for a projected five-year projected time period of Pt 2021-
22 through Ft 2025-26 for the projection of sewer rate revenue adjustments. Reviewing a multi-
year time period is recommended in order to more easily identify any major expenses that may
be on the horizon and also help detect any key cost trends that may be occurring. By anticipating
future financial requirements, the City can begin planning for these changes sooner, thereby
minimizing short-term rate impacts and minimizing overall long-term rate volatility.

The second step in determining the revenue requirement was to decide on the basis of
accumulating costs. For the City’s sewer revenue requirement analysis, a “cash basis” approach
was utilized, This method is the most commonly used methodology by municipal utilities to set
their revenue requirement. The actual revenue requirement developed for the City was
customized to follow their system of accounts (budget documents). However, the revenue
requirement still contains the basic cost components of a cash basis methodology.

 Rate Funding
A general financial guideline states that, at a minimum, a utility should fund an amount from
rates which is equal to or greater than the annual depreciation expense. Annual depreciation
expense reflects the current investment in plant being depreciated or “losing” its useful life.
Therefore, this portion of plant investment needs to be annually funded to maintain the existing
level of infrastructure. In addition, consideration should be given to using rate revenues to fund
an amount greater than the annual depreciation expense for repairs and replacements as costs
escalate over time and replacement cost is generally greater than the original cost. Whenever
possible, the City should be funding capital projects from rates in an amount greater than annual
depreciation expense to better reflect replacement costs. At the present time, the annual
depreciation expense of the sewer utility is approximately $378,000 based on the City’s financial
statements. Over the course of the five-year review period, the City is funding a total of $2.0
million via rates, or an average of $383,000 per year. With the proposed rate funding included
within this study, the sewer utility has made significant strides toward adequate funding for the
repair and replacement of the existing sewer system infrastructure.

Reserve Funding
The use of reserves to fund capital improvements is another method available to the City, when
and if reserves are available. During the projected time period of the rate study, there will be
approximately $462,000 in reserves used as a funding source for capital improvement projects
over the review period. The sewer utility reserve fund has historically been established by annual
surpluses in years where revenues may be greater than the annual expenses of the sewer utility.
This allows the City to reserve funds for projects in later years when more or larger projects are
undertaken. This approach helps to mitigate future rate adjustments and smooth rates over time.
However, close attention should be given to the reserve balance as to not reduce it below the
minimum target.

Long-Term Debt
The use of long-term debt is another potential source of funding for capital projects. There are
advantages and disadvantages with the issuance of long-term debt and it is important to weigh
them when deciding whether to issue or not. Long-term debt does have prudent applications
whereby it acts as a financial device to spread the costs of a larger project, such as a new pump
station, over multiple years. Doing so then assigns the costs of the new facility to the customers
who are benefit from it over the life of the facility (so called “inter-generational equity”). For this
study, no additional long-term debt has been assumed.

As can be seen, there are multiple methods by which the City may fund their capital projects.
Each method has an impact upon the revenue requirements of the sewer utility.

3.3 Development of the Sewer Cost of Service
The establishment of cost-based and equitable rates was of paramount importance in the
development of the City’s sewer cost of service analysis. Meeting the legal requirements and
documenting the steps taken to meet the requirements, has been in the forefront with the recent
legal challenges in the State of California on utility rates. A focus has been given to meeting the
legal requirements of California Constitution article XIII D, section 6 (Article XIII D). A key
component of Article XIII 0 is the development of rates which reflect the cost of providing service
and are proportionally allocated among the various customer classes of service, and the
customers within each class, HDR would point out that there is no single methodology for
equitably assigning costs to the various customer classes. The Water Environment Federation
Manual of Practice #27 provides various methodologies which may be used to establish cost-
based rates. Unfortunately, Article XIII D is not prescriptive and does not provide a specific
methodology for establishing cost-based rates.

HOR is of the opinion that the proposed rates meet the legal requirements of Article XIII 0. HOR
reaches this conclusion based upon the following:

  property related service (i.e., sewer service). The proposed rates are designed to collect the

•  The revenues derived from sewer rates shall not be used for any purpose other than that
  for which the fee or charge is imposed. The revenues derived from the City’s sewer rates are

•  The amount of a fee or charge imposed upon a parcel or person as an incident of property

  The study has appropriately grouped customers into customer classes of service (residential,
  restaurants, hotel, theatre, etc.) that reflect the varying customer usage patterns and system

3.3.1  Overview of the City’s Current Sewer Rate Structure
As mentioned previously, the cost of service analysis was reviewed for appropriateness given the

sewer rates. It is important to note that the City does not have the ability to obtain metered
water consumption data, which is helpful in reviewing and developing an equitable allocation of
costs. Given these limitations and based on the current rate structure used by the City, an
approach was developed to review the proportionality, or cost comparison, of the rate structure.

 Just as in the sewer capital funding plan, there are numerous funding sources that can be used
to fund the capital projects. Among the methods that may be used to finance these saltwater
capital improvement projects are long-term debt, reserves, and rates. Historically the City has
primarily utilized rates and reserves to fund the capital improvements. As with the sewer utility,
based on the rate transition plan developed as part of this revenue requirement, the City is
projected to have adequate resources to provide funding for these capital projects. Provided
below is a summary of the typical funding sources the City has used, and will continue to use, to
fund the capital improvements over the next five year period.

Rate Funding
A general financial guideline states that, at a minimum, a utility should fund an amount equal to
or greater than annual depreciation through rates. Annual depreciation expense reflects the
current investment in saltwater plant being depreciated or “losing” its useful hfe. Therefore, this
portion of plant investment needs to be replaced to maintain the existing level of infrastructure.
While the general financial guideline suggests funding an amount at least equal to the
depreciation expense, consideration should also be given to funding within rates some amount
greater than the annual depreciation expense to reflect the cost of replacement. The
depreciation expense reflects the cost of infrastructure that was constructed, on average, 15 to
20 years ago. Funding for the replacement cost is prudent and minimizes costs/rates over time.
With that in mind, for this review period, the City has increased the level of rate funding for their
renewal and replacement projects. The City has increased the annual rate funding for capital
projects from $65,000 in FY 2020-21 to $185,000 by FY 2023-26. As a point of reference, the City’s
current annual depreciation expense for the saltwater system is approximately $55,000 as
provided in the City’s financial records for EN’ 2019-20. Given that, this study has greatly improved
the funding for renewal and replacement capital projects but is not at a level of funding for full
replacement cost.

Reserve Funding
Available reserve funds are another method of funding capital improvements. For the study,
there are no assumed uses of reserves as a funding source for capital improvement projects. This
reserve fund is typically funded by annual surpluses, just as in the sewer utility. Again, this allows
the City to reserve funds for projects in later years when more or larger projects are undertaken.
This approach helps to mitigate future rate adjustments and smooth rates over time. Over the
planning horizon, close attention should be given to the reserve balance as to not reduce fund
balances below minimum targets described below.

Long-Term Debt
Another potential funding source for capital projects is the issuance of long-term debt. While
there are certain advantages and disadvantages with the issuance of long-term debt, it is
important to weigh all of them when deciding whether to issue or not. Long-term debt is typically
not issued to fund renewal and replacement projects similar to those being proposed during this
time period. Rather, long-term debt is often issued for major capital projects which have an
immediate impact on rates and long-term debt is a financing mechanism to smoothly
finance/fund the major capital project. For this analysis, no new long-term debt is assumed over
the planning period.

5.3 Development of the Solid Waste Cost of Service
lust as with the sewer and saltwater, the cost of service analysis developed in the 2017 Study
and the assumptions were reviewed as part of this study. It is important to note, the City
contracts for solid waste collection and disposal services. Consequently, the City does not have
information available on customers in regards to the size of the solid waste container or the
number of pick-ups. Given this, the information necessary to identify the cost components
related to providing service to various types of customers is unavailable. it should also be noted
that information on actual waste generation by customer type is limited, as most collection and
disposal practices do not separate by customer type. For example, a utility typically does not have
information on the average tonnage collected from an individual restaurant or grocery store. At
best, some utilities may have total tonnage collected by residential or commercial in aggregate.

The City’s solid waste rate structure is further complicated by the fact that a customer may not
have a specified, or individual, solid waste disposal container. In many cases, multiple customers
dispose of their waste in a single solid waste disposal container. As such, the solid waste
contractor may collect waste multiple times a week, or even multiple times a day depending, on
the need and activities in the area, Given this, it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine those
customers that benefit from a specific container or need at the current time. As a result, the
ratios utilized in the 2017 study were maintained as they are based on estimates of waste
generation by customer type.

5.6 Rate Adoption
Proposition 218 outlines a specific process to legally adopt and implement the proposed sewer,
saltwater, and solid waste rates. The first requirement is that the rates must be cost-based and
proportional, which is the purpose of completing the rate study. Once the proposed sewer,
saltwater, and solid waste rates have been developed, a public process must be undertaken to
adopt the proposed rates. This began with the presentation of the proposed rates to the Avalon
City Council in April 2021. At this meeting, the City Council directed staff to mail the Proposition
218 notices shown in the Proposition 218 Appendix to the City’s customers which outlines the
  —
  -

proposed changes in rates. The notice also contains the time, date, and location of the public
hearing, which is shown in the Approved Notice Appendix. The City Council then held a public
hearing on June 1, 2021 to discuss the publicly noticed and proposed rates. Absent sufficient
written protest by customers, the City Council moved to adopt the proposed sewer, saltwater,
and solid waste rates as outlined in the customer notification over the next five-year period.

SUBJECT:  FY22 Proposed Budget Amendments

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a  resolution  authorizing  the  proposed  budget
amendments as outlined in this report.

BACKGROUND: On July 6, 2021, City Council adopted the City’s annual operating and capital
budget for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2022 (FY22), with General Fund appropriations
totaling $11,751,423. General Fund appropriations include the allocation equal to 22% of the
transient occupancy tax (TOT) collected by the City during the fiscal year to the Love Catalina
Island Tourism Authority (Love Catalina). The appropriations also include the additional half
percent (0.5%) of sales tax revenue collected by the California Department of Tax and Fee
Administration and passed through the City to the Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC). These
budgeted expenditures are set based on revenue estimates developed as part of the budget
process. In addition, Avalon Measure H, a ballot initiative approved on November 3, 2020,
authorized an additional tax for cruise ship, ferry, and aircraft passengers and mooring renters
that went into effect on April 1, 2022; however, the Measure H tax revenues and passed-through
expenditures to the CIMC were not included in the adopted budget.

REPORT SUMMARY: The adopted FY22 Budget estimates TOT revenues totaling $5,150,000,
or approximately 95% of the pre-COVID FY19 revenue amount, Based on this estimate,
allocations to the Chamber were budgeted to 10260-5650 totaling $1,133,000. TOT revenues
collected through June 7, 2022 reflecting transient rental activity through April 2022 total

 Budget Overview

  Budget Process
  Each year, the Avalon City Council adopts, by formal resolution, an annual budget. This document
 serves as a financial plan. identi’ing the projected allocation and application of resources over the
 budget cycle. The published Operating and Capital Budget is designed to present summary
 intbrmation about the City’s financial plans for the year in a user-friendly fonnat. The budget is
 organized by fund and department. Expenditures are displayed anti subtotaled by the following
 types: Salaries & Benefits; Maintenance & Operations; Contract Services; and Capital Outlays.

 Line—item budget development is accomplished through the City’s online budget system, which
 allows each department to build its budget using computerized worksheets. The individual
 departments are directly responsible for developing the Maintenance & Operations and Contract
Services expenditure budgets. The Salary & Benefit infonnation is calculated and entered
  by the
 Finance Department based on salary schedules and applicable memorandums of understanding.
All supplemental budget requests (e.g. new personnel, services, equipment) are presented
separately for City Manager’s review and approval before becoming part of the operating budget.
The Finance Director provides the City Manager with proposed revenue projections. These
revenue estimates are then reviewed with the department budget requests to determine available
funding levels for the fiscal year. The City Manager and Finance Director then hold meetings with
the departments to review the operating budgets and supplemental budget requests. Once the
budget data has been reviewed and any changes have been made by the Finance Department, a
proposed budget document is prepared. Atler review and approval by the City Manager, the
proposed budget document is presented to City Council. with at least one study session and public
presentation, prior to adoption. During the fiscal year. the budget can be amended as necessary
  by
City Council to meet the City’s needs. The City’s budget and fiscal policies outline internal
controls for transfers within budgeted accounts.

Basis of Accounting
The City’s accounting system is maintained on a fund basis, in accordance with governmental
accounting standards. Each of the City’s funds is considered a separate accounting entity with a
self-balancing set of accounts that records assets, liabilities, fund equity, revenues and expenditures.
Funds are established and segregated for the purpose of recording specific programs or attaining
certain objectives in accordance with special regulations restrictions, or limitations.

Funds are classified into one of three categories: goreriiineiitu/ (general fund, special revenues),
p)oprjLan  (enterprise and internal service), and flthtciwi (trust or agency). Governmental funds
account for activities generally associated with local government operations. Proprietary funds are
financed and operated in a manner similar to private business enterprises, where the intent to
  is
recover the costs of providing goods and services from users through charges for services. Fiduciary
funds are utilized in situations where the government is acting in a fiduciary capacity as a trustee.

All governmental funds are budgeted and accounted for using the modified accrual basis of
accounting. which recognizes revenues when they become susceptible to accrual (i.e. measurable
and available). Available means collectible in the current period or soon enough thereafter to be
used to pay Liabilities of the current period. Example of such revenues include property tax, sales
tax, and interest earnings. Expenditures are recognized when the fund liability is incurred.
Proprietary fund revenues and expenses are budgeted and accounted for on a full accrual basis.
Revenues are recognized in the period when earned and expenses are recognized when incurred.
The basis of budgeting is the same as the basis of accounting used in the City’s audited financial
statements. The following Classification of Funds describes, in detail, the various types of funds

 Budget and Fiscal Policies
CITY OF AVALON

  137
 The following policies outline the City of Avalon’s (City) guidelines for budgetary decision-making and
sets standards for sound budgetary practices and fiscal performance.
An adopted set of budget policies that are consistently followed will assist the City in achieving its current
and futLire goals in a fiscally responsible and sustainable manner. These policies establish guidelines for
devcloping and monitoring the City’s annual opeiating and capital budgets as recommended by the
Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) and the National Advisory Council on State and Local
Budgeting (NACSLB). This document shall be reviewed on an annual basis to reflect the highest
standards of fiscal management and the City’s budgetary goals.
The City’s budget and fiscal policies have bccn organized under the following components:
  A.  Accounting and Annual Reporting
  B.  Budget Process
  C.  Structurally Balanced Budget
  D.  Revenues
  E.  Expenditures
  F.  General Fund Reserves
  G.  Enterprise Fund ‘Working Capital Targets
  H.  Investment Policy
  I.  Investment Policy for Solid Waste Postclosure and Corrective Action Trust Fund

  138
 A. ACCOUNTING AND ANNUAL REPORTING POLICIES
  Purpose; The purpose of this policy is to ensure the proper recording of financial transactions and
  identify the parties responsible for financia] reporting.

  Background:
  The City’s Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) presents the government and its
  component units (entities for which the government is considered to be financially accountable)
  financial and operating activities. The City’s blended component units, although legally separate
  entities. are. in substance, part of the City’s operations and financial data from these units are
  combined with data of the City. The Citvs financial statements and accounting records are maintained
  in accordance with the recommendations of the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB).
  The government-wide financial statements report information on all of the non—fiduciary activities of
  the primary government and its component units. For the most part, the effect of inter—fund activity
  has been removed from these statements. Governmental activities, normally supported by taxes and
  inter-governmental revenues, are reported separately from business-type activities that rely, to a
  significant extent, on fees and charges for support.
  Separate financial statements are provided for governmental funds, proprietary funds, and fiduciary
  funds, even though the latter arc excluded from the government-wide financial statements. Major
  individual governmental funds are reported as separate columns in the fund financial statements. The
  government-wide financial statements are reported using the economic resources measurement focus
  and the accrual basis of accounting, as are the proprietary fund and fiduciary fund financial statements.
  Revenues are recorded when earned and expenses are recorded when a liability is incurred, regardless
  of the timing of related cash flows. Property taxes arc recognized as revenues in the year for which
  they are levied. Grants and similar items are recognized as revenue as soon as all eligibility
  requirements imposed by the providers have been met, As a general rule, the effect of inter-fund
  activity has been eliminated from the government-wide financial statements. Direct expenses have
  not been eliminated from the functional categories; however, indirect expenses and internal payments
  have been eli in i nated.
  Amounts reported as program revenues include: I) charges to customers or applicants for goods,
  services, or privileges provided; 2) operating grants and contributions; and 3) capital grants and
  contributions, including special assessments. Internally dedicated resources are reported as general
  revenues rather than program revenues. Likewise, general revenues include all taxes.
  Governmental fund tinancial statements are reported using the current financial resources
  measurement focLis and the modified accrual basis of accounting. Revenues are recognized as soon
  as they are both measurable and available. Revenues are considered available when they are collected
  within the current period or soon enough thereafter to pay liabilities of the cunent period. For this
  purpose, the City considers revenues available if they are collected within 60 days of the end of the
  current fiscal period. Expenditures generally are recorded when a liability is incurred, as under accrual
  accounting. However, debt service expenditures, as well as expenditures related to compensated
  absences are recorded only when payment is due.

  139
 Taxes, licenses and interest associated with the current fiscal period are all considered to be
susceptible to accrual and are therefore recognized as revenues of the current fiscal period. Only the
portion of special assessments receivable due within the current fiscal period is considered to be
susceptible to accrual as revenue of the culTent period. All other revenue items are considered
measurable and available only when the City receives cash.
The City reports the following governmental fund types:

  •  General Fund has been classified as a major fund and is used to account for resources
  traditionally associated with governments which are not required legally or by sound financial
  management to be accounted for in another fund.
  •  Special Revenue Funds account for proceeds of specific revenue sources that are legally
  restricted or otherwise designated for specific purposes.
  •  Nonmajor Funds is the aggregate of all the other government funds.
The City reports the following proprietary funds:
  •  Harbor Fund has been classified as an enterprise fund and is used to account for all harbor
  operations
  •  Sewer Fund has been classified as an enterprise fund and is used to account for the fees and
  services for the operation and maintenance of sewer system.
  •  Saltwater Fund has been classified as an enterprise fund and is used to account for the
  operation of the City’s saltwater pumping plants and systems.
  •  Solid Waste Fund has been classified as an enterprise fund and is used to account for the solid
  waste collection and disposal costs.
  •  General Administration. Insurance, and Vehicle Maintenance have been classified as internal
  service funds and are uscd to account for operations that provide services to other departments
  of the City on a cost reimbursement basis.
Additionally, the City reports its Success Agency activity in a Private-Purpose Trust Ftind.
Policy:
Each year an audit will be conducted by an independent Certified Public Accountant Finn (CPA
Firm). The selection of the independent CPA Firm shall he in conformance with the City’s
professional services bidding procedures. Generally, the City shall request bids for audit services no
less frequently than every five years. The CPA Finn shall provide the Cily Council with an Audit
Communication Letter addressing significant findings of the auditors in conjunction with their
opinion on the City’s Comprehensive Annual Financial Report. These reports shall be submitted to
the City Council within 60 days of receipt of the repor.
During the annual budget process, the City will make available a preliminaiy year end, unaudited,
General Fund fund balance. It should be recognized, however, that the balance provided is subject to
both unforeseen financial transactions ofa material nature and subject to findings of the independent
audit. An audit verified year-end balance should he available by the end of December. The City will
use generally accepted accounting principles in preparing its annual financial statements, and will
strive to meet the requirements of the GFOA’s Award for Excellence in Financial Reporting program.

  140
 B. BUDGET PROCESS
  Purpose:
  The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the preparation, adoption, and presentation
  of the City’s annual budget.

  Background:
  The City of Avalon operates on a fiscal year basis, starting July 1 and ending June 30. The budget is
  prepared by the Finance Dcpartmcnt with the support of each operating department under the direct
  supervision of the City Manager. The Finance Department is responsible for coordinating all revenues
  estimates contained in the budget. Estimates are reached by analyzing historical revenue history,
  national and local economic trends and indices, and development patterns in the local economy. The
  Finance Department also coordinates the development of the expenditure budgets with the support of
  each operating department and the City Manager.

  The budget is structured to separate operating and capital activity at the fund and department level.
  The operating budget is a guide for the receipt and disbursement of hinds used to provide daily,
  routine public services to the community. The operating budget is structured to include historical
  budget and actual revenues and expenditures, along with the eulTent revenue estimates and proposed
  expenditures required in order to implement and maintain services to the community. The Capital

 C. STRUCTURALLY BALANCED BUDGET

  Purpose:
  The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the City’s operating funds aimed at achieving
  and maintaining a structurally balanced budget. State law requires that the City adopts a balanced
  budget. However, a budget that is balanced by the state’s definition may not necessarily be structurally
  balanced or sustainable if recurring expenditures are covered by reserves or non-reculTing or highly
  volatile revenues. This policy supports the on-going financial stability of the City by advancing a
  more sustainable definition of a balanced budget a structurally balanced budget.
  —

  Background:
  This section defines key tcrnis related to a structurally balanced budget:

  Recurring Revenues are the portion of the City’s revenues that can reasonably be predicted to
  continue year-to-year, with some degree of predictability. Property taxes are an example ofa recurring
  revenue. Non-recurring Revenue are revenues that are one-time in nature and cannot be reasonably
  expected to continue year-to-year.

  Some revenue sources may have both recurring and non-recurring components. These sources require
  the City to exercise judgment in determining how much of the source is truly recurring. For example.
  the City regularly receives transfer fees for the sale of moorings in the harbor however, the amount
  receivcd varies year-to-year based on the value of moorings and number of sales. In this case, it may
  he prudent to regard unusually high transfer revenues as non-recurring revenue under the assumption
  that such rcvenues are unlikely to continue, making it imprudent to use them for recurring
  expenditures.

  Recurring expenditures appear in the budget each year. Salaries, benefits, rent, utilities, maintenance
  costs and certain contracted services are common examples of recurring expenditures. In general,
  recurring expenditures should be those that the City expccts to fund every year in order to maintain
  culTent service levels. Non-recurring expenditures comprise special projects such as capital
  improvements, asset acquisitions, and other costs incurred infrequently by the City. In general, the
  City has a greater degree of flexibility to defer non-recurring expenditures than recurring ones.

  Reserves are the portion of fund balance set aside as a hedge against risk. The City has defined a
  minimum amount of funds it will hold in reserve. This serves as a “bottom line measure” to help
  determine the extent to which the City’s structural balance policy is being met if reserves are
  —

  maintained at their desired levels, it is an indication that the City is maintaining a structurally balanced
  budget. If reserves are declining, it may indicate an imbalance in the budget (e.g. ifreserves are being
  used to fund on-going expenditures). Desired reserve levels are further discussed in Sections F and G
  of this document.

  Policy:
  The City shall endeavor to adopt a structurally balanced budget. Generally, this means that recurring
  expenditures should he covered by recurring revenues and that non-recurring revenues should be used

  142
 to fund non-reclining expenditures. The Finance Department shall incorporate information into its
budget presentation demonstrating the Citys progress in achieving a structurally balanced budget.

In order to achieve a structurally balanced budget, the City should consider the following:

  Employee compensation and non-recurring revenues  —  With limited exceptions. non
  recurring revenues and reserves should not be used to fund employee compensation. One such
  exception might he a severe economic downturn where non-recurring revenues are
  temporarily used to ease the transition to an expenditure structure that is in line with new
  economic realities. Even this should only he done in the context ofa plan to return to structural
  balance and replenish any reserves that had been used.
  •  Operating and maintenance costs of capital assets purchased with non-recurring
  revenues While capital assets are often funded with non-recurring revenues, the City shall
  —

  be observant of the long-terni operating and maintenance costs of such purposes, to prevent
  the creation of new on-going expenditures that cannot be maintained by recurring revenues.
  •  Replacement of short-lived assets and non-recurring revenues The City shall prioritize
  —

  the use of non-recurring revenues to replace cutTent assets that have outlived their useful Lives
  over the purchase of entirely new assets. where the replacement of the expired or obsolete
  assets is critical to the maintenance of the City’s core programs. A replacement schedule for
  such assets is a good indicator of when to budget for these items.

 D. REVENUES

  Purpose:
  The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for (a)the development of revenue estimates, kb)
  fee structures, and (c) use of new recurring and non-recurring revenues in order to achieve a
  structurally balanced budget.

  Background:
  Revenue prQjections and assumptions are critical to budget decisions, particularly in order to achieve

  of the City’s key revenues arc subject to significant fluctuation dependent on a number of economic

  environment, it is important to have a consistent approach to projecting revenues in order for decision-
  makers to undcrstand the basis used to project the resources available for the budget. Revenue should
  be projected in a way that is not likely to lead to a revenue shortfall, hut also not to he so conservative
  that the projections consistently and substantially underestimate revenues.

  The City utilizes user charges and fees to help fund services. When certain services provided

  By definition. non-recurring revenues cannot he relied upon in future budget periods. Non-recurring

  Policy:
  The following guidelines are to be considered with regards to City re enues:

  a. Development of Revenue Estimates The City will estimate revenues using an objective and
  —

  h. Fee Stnictimm’e The City will comply with all applicable laws regarding the designation and
  —

  assessment of fees for services and other fees. The City’ vi11 calculate the full cost of providing a

  The City should consider reviewing and updating charges and fees periodically based on factors

   such as the impact of inflation, other cost increases, adequacy of cost recovery, use of services,
  and competitiveness of current rates.

c.  Use ofM’ir Recutt/iig and Ani-Reciuring Revenues Non-recurring revenues should be used to
  —

  hind non-recurring expenditures only. The City should dedicate new recurring revenue sources in

  1, Fixed cost increases, including built-in contract escalators, and benefit increases outside

 F. GENERAL FUr4D RESERVES

  Purpose:
  The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the General Fund’s unrestricted fund balance
  to improve and maintain the City’s financial stability in order to protect the City from unforeseen or
  unbudgeted situations (e.g. natural disasters, major infrastructure failures, unexpected litigation).

  Background:
  Fund balance serves as a measure of the financial resources available in a governmental fund. It is
  essential that govcrnments maintain adequate levels of fund balance to mitigate current and future
  risks (e.g. revenue shortfalls and unanticipated expenditures) and to ensure stable tax rates.

  In February 2009, the Governmental Accounting Standards Board issued GASB Statement No. 54,
  Fund Balance Reporting and Goieni,nenial Fund flpr’ Definitions, which separates fund balance
  into five separate categories based on the type and source of constraints placed on how resources can
  be spent. Prcsented in descending order from most constraining to least constraining, they include:
  nonspendable fund balance, restricted fund balance, committed fund balance, assigned fund balance,
  and unassigned fund balance. The total amounts in the Inst three categories (where the only constraint
  on spending, if any, is imposed by the government itself) is termed unrestricted fund balance. GASB
  Statement No. 54 recommends  “. ..at a minimum, that general-purpose governments, regardless of
  size, maintain unrestricted fund balance in their general fund of no less than two months of regular
  general fund operating revenues or regular general fund operating expenditures. The choice of
  revenues or expenditures as a basis of comparison may be dictated by what is more predictable in a
  government’s particular circumstances.”

  The adequacy of unrestricted fund balance in the General Fund should take into account the City’s
  unique circumstances and the City should consider the following factors to assess the adequacy of
  unrestricted fund ha lance:
  • Predictability of its revenues and olatility of its expenditures;
  • Perceived exposure to significant one-time outlays:
  • Potential drain upon General Fund resources from other funds, as well as the availability of
  resources in other funds;
  • Potential impact on the entity’s bond ratings and the corresponding increased cost of borrowed
  funds:
  • Commitments and assignments included in the unrestricted fund balance

  Policy:
  The City of Avalon will strive to maintain an unrestricted fund balance equal to no less than six (6)
  months of regular General Fund operating expenditure budget. The regular operating expenditure
  budget includes all cumTent operating expenditure appropriations, excluding capital outlays and other
  one-time discretionary payments.

  Visitor-driven tax revenues (e.g. transient occupancy tax, sales tax, admission tax) account for the
  majority of the City’s General Fund revenues, \vith the predictability of these revenues dependent on

  148
 overall tourism demand. Due to its unique Location, City revenues are particularly vulnerable to
disruptions to leisure travel and tourism caused by pandemics or other natural disasters. In addition,
the City is responsible for managing multiple enterprise funds, with operating expenditures
comparable in size to its General Fund. and the City needs to maintain reserves in order to cover
immediate capital needs. if working capital is not sufficient in those funds.

Funds appropriated from unrestricted fund balance should be appropriated for non-recurring
expenditures, as they represent prior year surpluses that may or may not materialize in subsequent
years. However, draws from unrestricted fund balance below the six month target amount or to cover
recurring operating costs are generally reserved for emergency or unforeseen situations but may be
accessed by Council by simple budget appropriation. Examples of situations may include but not
limited to the following:
  A. Sudden and unexpected significant facility failure that presents an immediate public safety
  concern to the community;
  B. Declaration of a State of Emergency by the Governor;
  C. Unanticipated expenditures as a result of legis]ative changes from State/Federal governments
  in the current fiscal year;
  D. Acts of Terrorism declared by the Governor or the President of the United States;
  F. Acts of nature, which are infrequent in occurrence; or
  F. Other emergency as defined by City Council

If unrestricted fund balance is to be used to fund recurring operating expenditures or if unrestricted
fund balance falls below the minimum threshold, the Finance Director shall recommend and submit
to City Council a plan to replenish reserves to minimum levels. This plan will specify the source of
funding and timeframe for replenishment. Reserves should he replenished within three years, if
possible.
